result:
There is a specific kind of quiet that only exists at 7:13 in the morning.

It’s not the deep quiet of 3 a.m., which feels ancient and empty, and it’s not the quiet of noon, which is really just noise you’ve learned to ignore. The morning quiet is different. It’s expectant. The kettle hasn’t boiled yet. Your phone is face-down on the nightstand, still warm from charging. Outside, the light is deciding what color it wants to be. And for about forty-five seconds after you open your eyes, before the memory of who you are and what you have to do today rushes back in, you are nobody in particular. You are just a consciousness waking up in a soft bed on a small planet.

I love that moment. I think about it a lot.

We don't talk enough about how strange it is to be alive right now. Not in a dramatic, existential-crisis way, but in a practical, logistical way. You are the result of an unbroken chain of people surviving. Every single one of your ancestors, back through plagues and famines and wars and ice ages and predators with teeth, managed to live long enough to have a child. Not one of them failed. If any one of them had slipped on a rock or taken a different road or decided not to talk to that stranger at the market, you wouldn’t be here reading this.

And now here you are, with a supercomputer in your pocket that can show you the surface of Mars or teach you how to make sourdough or translate a poem written in 12th-century Japanese. You can talk in real time to someone in Reykjavik while sitting in your kitchen in Ohio. A few hundred years ago, people died because they didn’t know they should wash their hands. Now we argue about whether the images generated by the machine in our pocket look real enough.

It’s absurd. It’s wonderful.

I’ve been thinking lately about libraries. Not the grand, institutional kind with marble columns, but the way we all carry invisible libraries around with us.

When I was a kid, my local library had that smell - paper and old carpet cleaner and the faint metallic tang of the date-stamp machine. I thought the library was the building. I didn’t understand that the real library was the system behind it: the Dewey Decimal numbers, the card catalogue, the patient librarians who knew that the book on volcanoes was probably shelved next to the book on earthquakes, and that if you liked Roald Dahl you would probably like Eva Ibbotson too.

Now we all live inside a library that builds itself while we walk through it.

Every conversation you’ve ever had, every half-remembered lyric, every argument you had in a car in 2009, every recipe your grandmother made without measuring - all of it is in there. And on top of that, there’s the other library, the external one, the one humanity has been writing for 5,000 years. The attempt to move an idea from one mind to another without it dying on the way.

Language is our oldest technology for that. It’s lossy and buggy and beautiful. We take this shimmering, complex feeling - grief, or awe, or the specific way light fell across your kitchen floor when you were seven - and we try to compress it into sounds we make with our mouths. And somehow, most of the time, it works. You say “I miss you” and another person, who has a completely different nervous system and childhood and set of anxieties, actually feels what you mean.

That has never not amazed me.

We’re told a lot these days that attention is broken. That we can’t focus anymore, that our brains have been rewired by feeds and infinite scroll. And there’s truth in that. The economy around us is very, very good at capturing attention. It has to be; attention is the only real currency.

But I think we also underrate how good humans are at paying attention when something actually matters. Watch someone who loves birds watch a tree. Watch a teenager learn a dance on TikTok and practice it for three hours until their calves ache. Watch a mechanic listen to an engine. That is not a broken attention span. That is attention so pure it looks like prayer.

Maybe the problem isn’t that we can’t pay attention. Maybe it’s that so much of what is clamoring for our attention isn’t worthy of it.

I read once about the way oysters make pearls. It isn’t a graceful process. A grain of sand, or a parasite, gets inside the shell and irritates the soft tissue. The oyster can’t get it out. So it does the only thing it can do: it coats it in layer after layer of nacre, that smooth, luminous stuff. Over years. It doesn’t remove the irritation. It transforms it.

People are like that too, I think. We all have that grain of sand. A worry we can’t solve, a memory that catches, a question we can’t answer about whether we’re living the right life. Most of our most interesting work comes from coating that irritation in layers. A song, a garden, a well-organized spreadsheet, a kindness to a stranger - all different kinds of nacre.

For a long time I thought you needed to have a Grand Purpose. Capital G, Capital P. A calling. Some people do. But for most of us, I think life is quieter and more piecemeal than that. It’s not one big purpose, it’s a thousand small devotions. Making your apartment feel like a place someone would want to come home to. Learning how to properly sharpen a knife. Remembering your friend’s mom’s surgery date. Trying, and failing, and trying again to keep the basil plant alive on the windowsill.

There’s a concept in Japanese called “ikigai” that got very popular in Western self-help books a few years ago. The books showed it as a Venn diagram: what you love, what you’re good at, what the world needs, what you can be paid for. Find the overlap in the middle and you’ve found your reason for living.

I love Venn diagrams. But real life is messier than that. Your ikigai might be that you make excellent pancakes and your kids love Saturday mornings because of it. It might be that you are the person in your office who always knows how to fix the printer. It might be that you walk your elderly neighbor’s dog. It doesn’t have to be monetizable. It doesn’t have to scale. It just has to be yours.

One of my favorite little facts: trees in a forest communicate through an underground network of fungi. They call it the Wood Wide Web. Older, larger trees - the “mother trees” - will send nutrients through this fungal network to younger trees that aren’t getting enough sunlight. They will even send chemical warnings if insects are attacking. The forest isn’t just a collection of individual trees competing for light. It’s a community.

We like to think of ourselves as so separate, so individual. My goals, my brand, my path. But we are also mycorrhizal. We are constantly, invisibly feeding each other. The person who wrote the open-source code that lets your bank app work. The person who grew the carrots you ate last Tuesday. The person who decided to keep the park bench painted so you had somewhere to sit.

You will never meet most of the people who have kept you alive.

And you will never meet most of the people you will keep alive, in small ways, without knowing.

If you’re reading this in that morning quiet, or the evening quiet, or on a crowded train where you’re trying to make the time pass - I hope you do something small and good with the next hour. Drink water. Text someone back. Look up at the sky and actually notice what the clouds are doing. Open a window. Let the air in your room change.

The world is very large and very old, and you are very small, but that is not a bad thing. Small things are the only things that fit in a human hand. Small things are what we are built to carry.

And if you have that familiar tug of anxiety, that low hum of “am I doing enough, am I enough, is any of this going to work out” - you are not alone in that. It’s part of the bargain of having a mind that can imagine the future. The oyster’s pearl starts with an irritation. The morning starts with a moment of being nobody. The book starts with a blank page.

We get to decide what layer we add next.
